# Verification, Feedback, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"*
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming* (1970) [@Dijkstra1970Notes]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's note.** Dijkstra's warning separates a check from the stronger claim
someone might attach to it. Passing tests supports only the conditions and
behaviors the tests exercised. A failed test can still decisively contradict a
bounded claim.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What signal came back from AI-assisted design work, what does it say about a
named action, artifact, assumption, or result, and what should the project
learn or change because of it?
:::

A returned signal does not explain itself. Architecture work receives signals
from tools and environments, human reviewers, learned methods, and deployed
systems or silicon. Verification does the claim-specific work of determining
whether a return is trustworthy and what, if anything, it can support.
Empirical checks qualify observed or computed quantities from runs, experiments,
prototypes, or deployed systems. Dynamic verification is one empirical form in
which tests, simulation, or emulation exercise an artifact and observe named
behaviors. Formal methods instead use mathematical models and logic to establish
the status of a property over a model under stated assumptions
[@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. These approaches are complementary, not
interchangeable. Feedback interprets the qualified result for the named object
and identifies the next justified action. Learning captures what the work
improves or retains because of that interpretation. A return may report a
measurement, expose a failure, localize a cause, challenge a rationale, or leave
a question unresolved. A recorded update is justified only when the record
names what produced the return, what it refers to, when it was obtained, and what
kind of update it supports.

Architecture studies combine empirical measurements, formal results,
simulation, physical analysis, model predictions, reviews, and field
observations. These signals do not share one meaning of *pass*, one type of
uncertainty, or one scope. An architect must qualify each return for the
property it can address, compare like with like, expose what remains unchecked,
and route the result without letting the signal decide its own use.

Generators may produce candidates faster, predictors may score them, and
optimizers may search directly against imperfect proxies. Generated
explanations can also sound more certain than the measurements allow. That
acceleration does not remove the property-specific verification obligation.
Each candidate still needs a check
with a declared property, an adequate reference or expected-result rule,
recorded conditions, and coverage. Generated tests or properties create their
own adequacy questions. Candidate production can scale while the work needed
to qualify a result remains the bottleneck. AI does not change what an
architecture result must contain.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Qualify returned fields as measurements, formal results, diagnostics, or
  unresolved signals while preserving lineage and execution status.
- Build matched comparisons with named candidates, comparators, quantities,
  conditions, uncertainty, and decision margins.
- Interpret empirical uncertainty and formal status without widening the
  property, assumptions, bounds, or coverage.
- Test proxies and explanations for support, numerical calibration, confounding,
  variability, selection bias, and robustness.
- Use qualified feedback to choose the next action and decide what to retain
  within a run, across a project, and for later work without turning every
  result into training data.

:::

## From Tool Return to Qualified Action {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

The environment described in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces
records whether a request was valid, what ran, what failed, which artifacts
returned, and what state and cost accompanied the attempt. This chapter begins
after that record exists. It asks
whether a returned field is valid for the requested quantity or property, what
claim that qualified result can support, and which technical action becomes
eligible.

A returned signal can support a project change only through a sequence of
claims. Qualification establishes what the return means, and the qualified
result supports a bounded claim. That claim makes an action eligible, so the
project can retain a change or lesson. A later step cannot repair a missing
earlier one.

Not every source returns a measurement. A review rationale, model
critique, proof status, counterexample, or tool warning may still be useful
when its source, target, scope, timing, and limitations are recorded. A
numerical return needs additional qualification before it can support a
comparison.

A failed setup is not a poor measurement of a candidate. It is no candidate
measurement at all. A clean process exit may still return a partial report,
omit a required field, use the wrong unit, or parse an unfamiliar warning as
success. A complete return can contain a genuine limit violation. Execution
status must survive intact so interpretation can distinguish these cases.

An incomplete attempt does not make every returned artifact unusable, but any
salvage is claim-specific. An individual field or artifact may proceed to
qualification only when the declared run specification and expected outputs
treat it as independently complete, its extraction and lineage are valid,
termination could not have changed its meaning or observation window, and the
claim does not depend on missing state. Otherwise, quarantine it with the
attempt.
Salvaging one field does not relabel the overall timed-out or incomplete
attempt as complete. Every other claim remains unresolved.

A reviewer must therefore keep five questions separate. Did the requested work
execute? Is the returned artifact structurally and semantically valid for its
intended downstream use? Is the measurement or formal result valid under its
stated conditions? Which requirement or check does it satisfy or contradict,
and what remains uncovered? What architecture conclusion or revision, if any,
does it support? A yes to any one question never answers those that follow.

Consider a generated RTL block. Its invocation may complete and return RTL,
logs, and a timing report. The RTL may parse yet fail elaboration or library
binding, or it may fail a downstream interface or semantic check. The artifact
is then invalid for its intended tool path. For an artifact that does elaborate,
a timing report may still leave endpoints unconstrained or use the wrong mode
or corner, which makes that result invalid for the timing claim. Even a
qualified timing result supports only the named timing requirement. Power,
functional correctness, and security remain uncovered, and the timing result
alone does not select the architecture.

A returned signal gains meaning only as it passes distinct, claim-specific
qualifications (@fig-evidence-flow). Result qualification first establishes
whether an artifact is usable downstream and binds the return to its type,
target, meaning, and conditions. Comparative measurements then need a matched
comparator, while a proof status, warning, review rationale, or counterexample
needs the check appropriate to that return. The side routes matter. An
incomplete return goes back to execution, and an invalid comparison or property
check goes back to study formulation.

![**A tool return gains meaning through claim-specific qualification.** The
execution record first supplies a return with status and lineage. Result
qualification binds its type, target, meaning, and conditions. A comparison
supporting a comparative claim adds a matched comparator; formal and other
returns follow the property check appropriate to their type. Feedback scopes
the interpretation of what the result supports and does not support before the
project records what to improve or retain.](images/F8-evidence-flow){#fig-evidence-flow
width="88%" fig-alt="A five-step flow from tool return through verification and
a comparison or property check to feedback and a learning step that records
what to improve or retain. Side paths send incomplete returns to execution
repair and invalid checks to study formulation."}

The check establishes the limit of the result. Feedback then states what the
qualified result supports, what remains open, and which object needs attention.
It does not prescribe its own update. Learning records what the current run,
project, or later work should improve or retain. That path also depends on what
produced the return, because different signal sources expose different
properties and limitations.

## Sources of Returned Signals

Human reviewers, architecture tools, learned methods, and deployed systems all
return signals. None combines complete context, immediate response, precise
localization, and decision-relevant coverage. Those differences determine what
later qualification must establish rather than creating one preferred source
(@tbl-feedback-sources).

| **Signal source** | **Common form** | **Timing and locality** | **Main quality question** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Human reviewer | Critique, rationale, missing constraint, or priority judgment. | Intermittent and often context-rich; locality depends on the review. | Does the reviewer have the relevant context, expertise, and authority, and is the rationale recorded? |
| Architecture tool or experiment | Scalar, trace, report, counterexample, diagnostic, or proof status. | Immediate to multi-day; may identify one path or only a terminal outcome. | Which property did the tool observe, under which conditions, with what coverage and error? |
| Learned model or method | Prediction, ranking, score, critique, or explanation. | Usually fast and dense; often tied to the supplied representation. | Does the predicted score agree with stronger checks in the region being used, and which assumptions does it share with the producer? |
| Deployed system or silicon | Telemetry, characterization result, incident, or user-visible symptom. | Delayed and sparse; often system-level rather than component-local. | Which population, version, workload, and unobserved causes limit the inference? |

: **Returned signals differ in form, timing, and locality.** Quality depends on
whether a signal is fit for the learning or revision it is asked to support.
{#tbl-feedback-sources tbl-colwidths="[18,25,27,30]"}

Fast, dense signals are often narrow or proxy-based. Direct field signals may
be delayed and confounded, while contextual review may be authoritative but
intermittent. An architect should therefore select and qualify a source for the
property and action at hand rather than treat speed, density, or direct
observation as evidence quality.

A delayed signal can resolve an outcome while teaching little about how to
revise the work. A three-day place-and-route and timing run may show that a
candidate missed timing, but the final result does not identify which of
thousands of generated choices caused the miss. Revision needs a signal at the
right locality, such as path slack linked to the graph node, parameter, or
transformation that changed.

Feedback engineering offers a useful precedent. It separates whether the state
needed for a corrective action is observable from the design of that action,
and it treats delay as part of the feedback path
[@AstromMurray2008FeedbackSystems]. A multi-day architecture tool return can
leave the cause of a failure only partially observable even when the final
outcome is clear. The analogy stops there. This chapter does not model design
search as a linear controller; it borrows the narrower lesson that available
signals and their delay limit which correction is justified.

Handling that delayed result begins with lineage rather than causal
attribution. Bind the return to the exact candidate, parent actions, represented
state, constraints, tool and checker versions, seed, checkpoint, workload, and
software conditions that produced it. Lineage alone does not qualify the
return. When execution, setup, extraction, and check conditions are valid, the
terminal result can establish that this candidate missed timing under those
conditions. It does not yet establish which earlier action caused the miss.

The next step is a distinguishing comparison. Inspect path endpoints,
constraint coverage, congestion, power-density maps, and the differences from
the parent or a matched sibling. A stale constraint or broken setup routes the
revision to the environment or representation. Repeated failure across a
matched proposal class, after shared setup and conditions are checked, can
justify reopening the method or study and asking whether the representation,
shared constraints, or proposal process needs to change. A localized mechanism
supported by the comparison can justify a design revision. If no diagnostic
separates those possibilities, preserve the terminal outcome and leave the
mechanism unresolved rather than turning every upstream action into a negative
label.

Deployment feedback follows the same rule. A field result attaches first to the
shipped hardware, software, workload, and operating conditions it observed.
Those conditions may reopen an earlier claim, but the field symptom does not
identify the responsible design choice until an additional comparison or
diagnostic supports that attribution.

Dense, immediate feedback is easier for a method to learn from, but it is often
a proxy. Feedback that observes a decision-relevant property may be slower,
more expensive, or less frequent. Fast proxy signals can guide search only
inside their validated range. Slower or less frequent checks can test
properties the proxy omits. Each signal should therefore be qualified by its
latency, granularity, execution cost, uncertainty, interpretation time, and
review cost.

Empirical returns take the first qualification path. The next question is
whether a numerical value is eligible to enter the comparison the architecture
claim requires.

## Qualifying Empirical Measurements

An empirical measurement is an observed or computed quantity from a run,
experiment, implementation flow, prototype, or deployed system under recorded
conditions. It may carry sampling variation, run-to-run variability, numerical
tolerance, and model error. Those limits differ from the logical status of a
formal result.

A measurement record needs enough information to answer six questions
(@tbl-measurement-record).

| **Field** | **Question the record must answer** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidate identity** | Which design revision, configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| **Quantity and unit** | What property was measured or computed, how was it aggregated, and in what unit? |
| **Conditions** | Which tool, model, configuration, corner, seed where relevant, and operating conditions apply? |
| **Extraction status** | Did the expected artifact exist, parse under the declared schema, and retain unfamiliar warnings? |
| **Variation and error** | What repetitions, sampling method, numerical tolerance, model error, or known bound limits the value? |
| **Source record** | Which returned artifact and execution attempt support the field, and can the value be recovered from them? |

: **A measurement needs identity, meaning, conditions, and limits.** These fields
test whether the execution record is sufficient for the comparison being
attempted.
{#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

A returned value can enter a comparison only when these fields make it
interpretable, bound its use, and keep it recoverable from the attempt that
produced it. They work together as an admission test, not as six independent
quality scores. Passing that test does not make the comparison valid. It makes
the value eligible to enter one.

For sampled workloads or repeated flows, the record also names the unit of
observation, target population, sampling window, aggregation, and dependence
structure. Missing or censored observations remain visible rather than
disappearing from the aggregate. These fields separate a quantity computed
correctly from an estimate that represents the population and decision the
study actually names.

The environment provides returned artifacts, extraction status, recorded
conditions, and lineage. Measurement qualification cannot reconstruct missing
versions or rerun a parser. It asks whether the quantity, aggregation, error,
comparator, and check scope make the returned field usable as a measurement.
Missing execution fields require an environment repair. Inadequate observations
or an invalid comparison require a change to the study.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A returned value must qualify before it becomes feedback"}
**Context.** Consider a prospective larger-L2 request under the fixed XR
workload and software state. One illustrative attempt ends in a stale-state
setup failure. A later illustrative summary reports a value but omits the raw
artifacts, parser status, and lineage. Neither case is retained execution
evidence.

**Required record.** Qualification needs the exact candidate, workload,
software, tool, and model identity; terminal status; raw return and extraction
status; units and conditions; and the uncertainty or bound that limits use of
the value.

**Action.** Route the stale-state failure to environment repair and retain its
failure class. Keep the later value unqualified until its missing record is
supplied. Reject no candidate from either case.

**Takeaway.** Chronology does not turn an infrastructure failure or an
unrecoverable summary into design evidence.
:::

Until those execution records qualify, neither a candidate outcome nor a
mechanism claim is supported.
Once a value is qualified, it can enter the comparison that the architecture
question requires. Qualification establishes what one return means.
Comparison establishes what differs between the candidate and a declared
alternative under matched conditions.

Empirical uncertainty and formal proof status answer different questions. An
empirical interval summarizes variation under a sampling and repetition
procedure. Its interpretation depends on the population, statistic, dependence
structure, model error, and decision margin. A formal result is not a narrow
empirical interval and has no sampling confidence level. It reports a logical
outcome for a stated property, model, and assumptions. Solver time, proof depth,
and memory limit its scope or completion, not its statistical confidence.
Formal returns therefore need a parallel qualification path over the stated
property, model, assumptions, and proof scope before comparison resumes.

## Formal Verification and Its Scope

### Formal Status and Counterexamples

Formal verification follows the same qualification path without becoming an
empirical measurement or necessarily requiring a matched comparator. Its
returned status begins with three objects. The *property* states the behavior
to check. The *model* defines the state, transitions, and artifacts over which
the property is interpreted. The *assumptions* restrict inputs, environment
behavior, reset, clocks, protocols, or neighboring components. A formal result
is meaningful only when all three travel with it. A proof over the wrong model
or under an impossible assumption can be logically sound and architecturally
useless.

The checked model may differ from the RTL or implementation artifact named in
the architecture claim. Elaboration, extraction, or abstraction may add or
remove behaviors. The result must state what correspondence the flow preserves
between the model and claimed artifact and why that relation lets the proved
property carry to the claimed artifact [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

The result also depends on a trusted checking base, the steps and components
that turn the architecture artifact and requirement into the problem the solver
actually checks. The record identifies elaboration or model extraction,
property translation, relevant libraries and scripts, the solver or proof
checker, and any certificate or replay path. A proof can be logically valid for
a mistranslated property or the wrong extracted model and still fail the
architecture requirement. When a tool produces a checkable proof certificate or
replay artifact, retain it. Some tools return no such artifact, so the record
must not imply that one exists.

The project record must distinguish whether the checker produced a proof, a
counterexample, a bounded-only result, or an inconclusive result. Each status
supports a different next action. A project cannot relabel one as another merely
because it needs an answer.

Counterexamples require one more distinction before they direct a repair. In
counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR), a counterexample that
exists only because the abstract model admits behavior excluded by the concrete
system guides refinement of the abstraction [@ClarkeEtAl2000CEGAR]. It is not
evidence that the design is wrong. A trace that survives concretization and
setup review may instead expose a real design defect or a requirement that was
written incorrectly. CEGAR is therefore a specific formal-verification
procedure, not a generic label for any feedback loop. The counterexample's
status determines whether the next action repairs the abstraction, the design,
or the requirement.

### Bounds, Progress, and Property Strength

Bounded model checking searches modeled traces through a finite bound $k$
under stated assumptions [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Failing to find a counterexample
through $k$ does not exclude a longer one. An unbounded safety conclusion
requires a completeness argument or an unbounded method such as induction or
a property-directed reachability method such as IC3
[@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR]. Even then, the result covers only the
stated property over the modeled transition system and assumptions.

Safety and liveness make different claims. A safety property excludes a bad
behavior, such as two requesters simultaneously holding exclusive ownership of
one cache line. Proving such a safety property without a bound still does not
establish progress. A liveness property requires progress, such as an accepted request eventually
receiving a response [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness;
@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A bounded response check can expose a slow or stuck
execution within its horizon, but it does not prove that starvation or deadlock
is impossible beyond that horizon. An unbounded progress claim needs a
liveness-capable proof or a justified reduction, and it must retain the
fairness assumptions that rule out indefinitely postponed actions. Unrealistic
fairness assumptions can hide an architectural progress defect. The result
therefore records the property class, fairness assumptions, proof method, and
any bound or reduction used.

A property can pass without checking the intended behavior. *Vacuity* occurs
when a condition that should trigger the property never occurs, so the
implication is always true [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity;
@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A nonvacuous property can still be weak. It may allow
a response thousands of cycles late, omit exclusivity, ignore reset, or check
one requester while leaving another unconstrained. Teams can exercise
properties with cover statements, reachable triggers, known positive and
negative cases, mutation, and review against the requirement they are meant to
express. Systems such as AssertLLM generate SystemVerilog assertions from
design specifications and evaluate them against golden register-transfer-level
(RTL) designs with formal property verification [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM]. If
the RTL and assertions inherit the same missing requirement, a clean proof
still says nothing about the omitted behavior.

Generated assertions are themselves verification artifacts that need to be
qualified. A study of LLM assertion generation reports that general-purpose
models produced substantial fractions of syntactically and semantically
incorrect assertions, while a task-specific fine-tuned model improved those
two dimensions [@PulavarthiEtAl2025AssertionGeneration]. A project must still
check syntax and elaboration, semantic strength, coverage of the intended
properties, and whether the assertions detect relevant seeded or retained
bugs. These checks make assertion generation more useful; they do not show that
the generated property set is complete.

### Equivalence, Refinement, and Composition

Equivalence checking asks whether two artifacts preserve a declared relation.
Combinational equivalence can pair state elements as cut points and compare the
combinational logic between them. Sequential equivalence is needed when
transformations such as retiming, latency changes, additional state, or a
changed reset mapping alter correspondence across state or time. Neither form
establishes that the reference artifact expresses the intended architecture
[@Kropf1999FormalVerification].

Equivalence is also too strong when an implementation intentionally adds
detail or permits fewer behaviors than an abstract specification. A refinement
check instead asks whether each implementation behavior allowed by the mapping
remains within the specification. Large proofs are often decomposed by
component. In an assume-guarantee argument, each block proves a guarantee only
while its environment satisfies named assumptions; the composition is sound
only when neighboring guarantees discharge those assumptions
[@BenvenisteEtAl2018Contracts]. A block proof does not silently become a
whole-system proof. The refinement mapping, component boundaries, assumptions,
and unproved remainder remain part of the result.

### Formal and Dynamic Coverage

A reviewer must also be able to trace each architectural requirement to the
property or relation meant to cover it. The record connects the requirement
source and claimed RTL or implementation artifact to the checked model,
property or relation, assumptions, and abstraction or extraction relation. It
also identifies elaboration or model extraction, property translation, relevant
libraries and scripts, the solver or proof checker, and any checkable proof
certificate or replay artifact the tool provides. The reviewer also needs the
proof method and status, bound or completeness basis, vacuity or cover evidence,
refinement or composition boundary, and explicitly uncovered remainder. Even a
clean set of proofs does not establish that the property set is complete.

Dynamic simulation makes a different claim. Directed tests,
constrained-random stimuli, coverage-guided generation, emulation, formal
methods, and post-silicon testing complement one another because exhaustive
simulation is generally infeasible [@Kropf1999FormalVerification]. Code
coverage reports exercised structures. Functional coverage reports events or
bins defined by the verification plan. SystemVerilog defines
functional-coverage constructs such as
covergroups, coverpoints, bins, and crosses [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. Neither
coverage family reports the fraction of every reachable behavior checked, while
a formal proof covers no property that was never written.

Published accounts of the Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) failure
document both the missing table entries and Intel's \$475 million pretax charge
[@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Pentium FDIV bug and the limit of sampled testing"}
**The claim.** Pre-silicon testing supported the implemented floating-point
division behavior over the cases it exercised.

**The gap.** Five missing table entries escaped testing and produced incorrect
results for rare operand pairs. Intel later reported a \$475 million pretax
charge for replacement and associated costs.

**The lesson.** Passing sampled tests cannot establish the absence of all
failures. Another check is needed when the property demands one.
:::

Formal verification later became the primary validation method for the
execution cluster in Intel's Core i7 flow [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal]. With
that parallel qualification path established, the four formal statuses map to
distinct technical actions (@tbl-formal-result-status).

| **Formal status** | **What it establishes** | **Eligible next action** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proved** | The declared property or equivalence holds for the recorded model and assumptions, conditional on the property translation, model-to-artifact relation, trusted checking components, and available certificate or replay path. A proof method need not be complete for a proved result to be valid. | Record the scoped result and discharge only the claim covered by that property, model, assumptions, and proof mode. |
| **Counterexample** | A modeled trace violates the property. Setup, assumptions, and concretization still determine whether the trace represents a realizable architecture failure. | Refine the abstraction when CEGAR identifies a spurious trace; otherwise repair the design or requirement that a reviewed realizable trace contradicts. |
| **Bounded-only** | No counterexample was found through the declared horizon. Nothing is established beyond that bound without a separate completeness argument. | Record the bound, extend or change the checking method when the broader claim matters, or leave that claim open. |
| **Inconclusive** | The solver supplied neither a proof nor a counterexample because it returned `unknown`, exhausted resources, or failed to complete the proof procedure. | Revise the abstraction, assumptions, proof method, or resource budget. Do not report the result as a pass. |

: **Formal status determines what can happen next.** A proof discharges only its
scoped claim, while counterexamples, finite bounds, and incomplete proofs require
different repairs or leave broader claims open.
{#tbl-formal-result-status tbl-colwidths="[16,45,39]"}

Matched empirical comparison follows a different qualification path. Its claim
depends on a declared comparator, conditions, and uncertainty rather than formal
proof scope.

## Building Matched Architecture Comparisons {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

Architecture decisions usually depend on differences rather than isolated
values. A cache study asks how a candidate differs from a baseline under the
same workload and software state. Two candidates produced by different
processes can also be compared here, but the result is limited to their
measured design difference rather than the quality of the complete workflows
that produced them. The comparator is part of the claim, not a footnote added
after the result.

A comparison binds explicit candidate and comparator revisions to one measured
difference and to the conditions that limit it (@fig-claim-frame).

![**A comparison binds two designs to one measured difference and its
limits.** Candidate and comparator are evaluated for the same quantity and
unit. The result remains conditional on workload and state, tool conditions,
uncertainty, and the property the check can observe.](images/F7-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame
width="100%" fig-alt="Three-column comparison frame. Candidate
and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty, which
are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

Changing the workload, design state, tool conditions, uncertainty model, or
observable property creates a different comparison even when the center value
is unchanged. Those bindings prevent a numerical difference from carrying into
conditions or claims that were never measured.

For matched cases $c_j$, the basic paired difference is

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j).
$$

The sign convention must be stated. Positive may mean improvement for
throughput and regression for latency. A percentage must name its
denominator. An aggregate must state whether it is a mean, percentile, maximum,
geometric mean, or another statistic. For positive ratios normalized to a
reference, the geometric mean preserves the relative interpretation across a
benchmark set; an arithmetic mean of those ratios can depend on which system is
chosen as the reference [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]. Without those choices,
two correct numbers can still form an incoherent comparison.

### Matching Factors That Can Change the Result

The candidate and comparator should differ only along the factors the study
intends to compare. Workload, software, model version, tool flags, operating
point, warmup, sampling window, and resource budget can all create a
difference that has nothing to do with the architecture change. A matched
comparison records them rather than relying on similar filenames or a shared
directory.

Systematic model error sometimes cancels in a relative comparison. It does so
only when the model treats the candidate and comparator similarly in the
region being studied. A frozen simulator can support an ordering even when its
absolute prediction differs from silicon, but that bargain fails when the
architecture change crosses an unmodeled boundary or affects one candidate
differently. Cancellation is a hypothesis to check, not a property of using
the same tool [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError;
@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity].

### Differences and Their Uncertainty

Repeated measurements estimate run-to-run variability when the flow or
workload is variable. Paired resampling can preserve the relationship between
matched baseline and candidate frames.[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07] The
resampled object is the paired-difference sequence $d_j$, not two independently
resampled streams. The resulting interval assumes that this sequence is
sufficiently stationary over the sampled region and that the declared block
length preserves the dependence relevant to the statistic. Numerical
tolerances, finite sampling, heuristic variation, and model error may require
different treatments. One generic error bar cannot represent all of them.

[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07]: **Paired block resampling**: A block bootstrap
resamples contiguous segments of the paired-difference sequence. Pairing keeps
each baseline and candidate case together, while blocks preserve local
dependence under the method's assumptions [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap].

Consider a future, fully retained matched run that defines improvement as
baseline latency minus candidate latency, so a positive value means the
candidate is faster. Suppose its point estimate were 0.3\ ms and its 95 percent
interval ran from -0.1\ ms to 0.7\ ms. These are invented teaching values, not
measurements reported by this book or derived from a retained Lighthouse
run. If the future run retained matched frame sequences and used a
declared paired block-resampling procedure, the interval would span both a
small regression and a larger improvement. Because it includes zero, that
hypothetical comparison would leave the tail-latency question unresolved even
though the point estimate is favorable.

A decision margin adds a second test. If the study requires an improvement of
at least $m$, the comparison must resolve the result relative to $m$, not
merely relative to zero. A difference inside known measurement resolution or
uncertainty remains unresolved. Calling it a tie may be appropriate under a
predeclared rule, but calling it an improvement is not.

### Controlling Confounding and Selection

A matched comparison can still support the wrong explanation. Confounding
exists when another changed factor could account for the result. Stable
versions, ablations, matched contrasts, and sensitivity studies help separate
the intended change from plausible alternatives.

Selection introduces another problem. If a search evaluates many noisy
candidates and reports only the best, the selected value retains some of the
luck that made it win. Repeating the same search data does not remove that
bias [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. A fresh evaluation should measure the
chosen candidate again on seeds, workloads, or cases that did not select it.
That evaluation asks whether the margin survives after the search has stopped
choosing the winner.

Even a carefully matched comparison may rely on a proxy that does not carry to
the intended architecture result. A favorable outcome also does not establish
the proposed mechanism. Proxy qualification and mechanism testing therefore
need separate checks after candidate and comparator conditions have been
matched.

## Qualifying Proxies and Testing Explanations {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

A cheaper signal must track the architecture quantity closely enough for the
decision being made. The proposed mechanism must separately explain the
observed outcome. A qualified proxy cannot answer the mechanism question by
itself.

### Qualifying a Proxy for the Decision

An architecture proxy is useful because it is cheaper or earlier than the
quantity that ultimately matters. Estimated instructions per cycle (IPC),
analytical energy, wirelength, congestion, utilization, and cycle counts can
all help order candidates. They remain partial measurements. The danger grows
when an optimizer searches directly against them, because the search is
rewarded for finding every region where the proxy and the intended result part
company.

This is Goodhart's problem in architecture form. A measure that once tracked a
goal can stop tracking it after it becomes the optimization target
[@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. AI is not unique in
this behavior. It changes the scale and persistence of the search for
loopholes.

Observed qualification cases and held-out agreement answer separate questions
(@fig-trust-calibration). Finite cases directly establish only sampled points or
strata in named workload, candidate, tool, and condition dimensions. The
schematic therefore separates observed strata from an internal gap and from
extrapolation beyond the sampled range.

*Proxy qualification* covers several relationships that must remain distinct.
Numerical calibration is only a declared mapping between proxy outputs and
stronger reference outcomes. Confidence calibration instead asks whether stated
probabilities or intervals match observed frequencies and remains a
system-evaluation question in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. Observed
qualification coverage records the sampled dimensions, strata or cases, and
gaps. Held-out error, ranking stability, uncertainty, and fitness for the
architecture decision require separate tests.

![**Discrete qualification cases leave visible gaps.** The conceptual,
normalized curves show paired proxy and stronger-reference observations in
three sampled strata, an unsampled gap between them, and possible divergence as
search continues beyond those strata. A real study must record the dimensions,
sampled cases or strata, gaps, and held-out agreement; these curves are not
measured data.](images/F9-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="100%"
fig-alt="Conceptual normalized plot with three separate green qualification
strata in the left-hand range. Paired proxy and stronger-reference markers
appear in each stratum, while a dashed white band marks an unsampled gap between
the first two. The curves may diverge as search continues into an unqualified
right-hand range; no plotted curve is measured data."}

The internal gap remains unqualified even though both smooth curves pass
through it. Held-out comparisons must still establish whether error and
candidate ordering are adequate at the sampled strata. Moving into the gap or
beyond the observed range requires new reference checks or a separate
justification. The possible divergence on the right is the practical warning.
A higher proxy score outside qualified support is not automatically a stronger
architecture result.

SMARTS provides one specific precedent for population inference. Rigorously
sampled intervals from a declared benchmark execution stream can support
quantified performance estimates for the declared execution population
[@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. That result does not make an arbitrary held-out
sample representative. A new architecture study must declare its own target
population and justify a sampling design for that population. Its inference
does not extend to workload, candidate, tool, or condition regions outside
those declarations.

Numerical calibration and ranking fidelity answer different questions. A
numerically calibrated scalar mapping relates proxy outputs to reference
outcomes under a declared procedure, while a predictive interval adds a stated
uncertainty model [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Ranking fidelity asks
whether candidate ordering survives the stronger check. Low average error can
coexist with the wrong ordering near the decision boundary, while a useful
ordering can coexist with biased absolute values. Qualification therefore
reports the relationship needed by the decision and tests its error or
instability against the declared margin.

A proxy can fail in several ways, and each failure removes a different
inference. The six problems therefore need separate tests
(@tbl-proxy-diagnostics).

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proxy mismatch** | Compare the proxy with a more decision-relevant measurement on matched cases. | The available evidence does not support carrying the proxy result to the stronger claim. |
| **Observed qualification coverage** | Record the workload, candidate, tool, and condition dimensions; place matched cases across sampled strata; and identify gaps the search may enter. | The available evidence does not qualify a reported candidate outside sampled cases or inside an unqualified gap. |
| **Held-out agreement** | Measure error, ranking stability, and uncertainty against the decision margin on cases not used to fit or tune the proxy. | The available evidence does not support reliable candidate ordering for the declared use, even at observed qualification cases. |
| **Confounding** | Hold versions and budgets fixed, use matched contrasts, and test plausible alternative causes. | The difference does not identify the proposed cause. |
| **Variability** | Repeat stochastic flows or sampled workloads and report dispersion or ranking stability. | The point estimate may not resolve the declared margin. |
| **Selection bias** | Re-evaluate the selected candidate on fresh cases not used to choose it. | The apparent margin may contain the luck that made the candidate win. |

: **Each weakness requires a different diagnostic.** A second run cannot repair
a missing property, and a stronger tool cannot repair an unmatched comparator.
{#tbl-proxy-diagnostics tbl-colwidths="[18,43,39]"}

The proxy first has to observe the relevant property, have matched
qualification cases where the search will use it, and preserve the ordering the
decision needs on held-out cases. Separate diagnostics must then rule on
alternative causes, run-to-run variation, and favorable noise retained when the
search selects its winner. An adverse result removes only the inference named in
the final column. It does not make the other diagnoses or repairs
interchangeable.

Robustness checks stress the current claim envelope rather than silently
widening it. Workload phases, seeds, nearby candidates, tool or model
alternatives, and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners can expose a
ranking or margin that depends on one favorable case. Sensitivity to those
declared factors narrows, contradicts, or supports the current result. A changed
objective or specification first reopens the proxy relationships that depend on
it. If the change alters what success means for the target decision, the old
qualification no longer answers the same question and must not be presented as
a robustness result.

The public debate over learned macro placement illustrates why qualification and
matched comparison matter. Proxy metrics such as wirelength and congestion do
not automatically settle post-route power, performance, and area, and public
assessments have differed in tool flow, baseline strength, pretraining, and
available design data [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement;
@GoldieEtAl2024AlphaChipAddendum; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment;
@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. The durable lesson is not a verdict on one
placement method. It is that a proxy comparison cannot silently inherit strength
from a stronger result obtained under unmatched conditions.

Qualified measurements still do not choose among performance, power, and area.
Each quantity retains its unit and uncertainty, and hard constraints remain
separate. Any aggregate ranking must declare its normalization, weights, or
dominance rule. If two candidates remain nondominated, the feedback exposes an
architecture tradeoff rather than manufacturing a winner
[@Deb2001MultiObjective].

A simulator can also be the exploited reference. In Gupta et al.'s
architecture-agent study, a ChampSim assertion against last-level-cache write
bypass was eliminated by the optimized build, so that configuration did not
enforce the intended correctness constraint [@GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent].
Qualifying a proxy against that run would reproduce the blind spot. The reference check
must itself retain the property, configuration, and coverage used to justify
it.

### Separating the Outcome From the Mechanism

An outcome says what changed. A mechanism says why. They require different
comparisons and can reach different statuses.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A lower miss count is not the architecture result"}
**Context.** A future Lighthouse cache run could measure 99th-percentile frame
time and capacity misses under matched workload and software conditions. The
book reports no such execution result.

**Required distinction.** A lower miss count would support an intermediate
cache effect only after qualification. Establishing a frame-time outcome and
showing that fewer misses caused it require separate comparisons.

**Action.** Preserve the intermediate effect if qualified, leave the frame-time
comparison unresolved when its interval crosses zero, and add a distinguishing
mechanism check before that explanation guides another design change.

**Takeaway.** An intermediate measurement cannot fill an unresolved
architecture outcome or mechanism claim.
:::

The reverse can also occur. A candidate may improve the measured outcome while
the proposed explanation fails. The improvement can remain a valid observation
if the comparison is sound, but an unresolved or contradicted mechanism should
not guide the next change. A plausible model explanation is a hypothesis, not
a substitute for a contrast.

Useful mechanism checks include matched workload contrasts, ablations,
counterfactual configurations, traces of the affected events, and sensitivity
around the changed parameter. They should be declared before the result when
possible. Otherwise, an explanation can be fitted to any outcome after the
fact. A contrast identifies a cause only when the intervention is well defined
and plausible alternative paths are ruled out by the design or bounded by
explicit identification assumptions [@Pearl2009Causality]. The resulting
judgments must remain separate even when they come from the same study
(@tbl-outcome-mechanism).

| **Question** | **Possible status** | **Architecture example** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Did the requested quantity change in the declared direction?** | Supported, contradicted, or unresolved within the stated comparison. | A latency interval that includes zero leaves the claimed improvement unresolved. |
| **Did the proposed intermediate effect occur?** | Supported, contradicted, unresolved, or not tested. | A qualified reduction in capacity misses supports a bounded cache effect. |
| **Did that intermediate effect cause the outcome?** | Supported only by a distinguishing intervention or contrast under stated identification assumptions; otherwise unresolved. | Lower miss count alone does not establish that it caused a tail-latency change. |
| **What did the check not observe?** | Explicit nonclaims. | A cache-local result does not establish thermal behavior, voltage-droop behavior, functional correctness, security, or system-level XR quality. |

: **Outcome and mechanism remain separate results.** A supported intermediate
effect cannot fill an unresolved architecture comparison.
{#tbl-outcome-mechanism tbl-colwidths="[26,30,44]"}

Evidence need not resolve these questions together. An outcome and an
intermediate effect may resolve while the proposed cause remains open, and a
supported cause cannot widen the set of properties the check observed. A local
cache result can therefore guide the next cache experiment without becoming a
claim about thermal, electrical, functional, security, or system behavior.

This separation makes negative results useful. A contradicted mechanism can
improve the architecture model even when the candidate result is favorable. A
resolved regression can rule out a design direction. An unresolved comparison
can reveal that the observation budget or measurement plan was too weak. None
of those outcomes is a failed study if the record keeps them distinct.

## Matching Checks to Claims {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

A supported difference is not the same as adequate requirement coverage. Each
material architecture requirement needs a suitable check path, and those paths
together must cover the claim.

Assurance engineering connects a claim to the checks and assumptions that
support it [@Kelly2004GSN]. A cumulative study record can preserve that
connection without imposing a second project process or reducing the result to
one confidence score. For each claim, the record names the property and scope,
check coverage and possible error direction, shared assumptions, formal proof
status where applicable, empirical and model uncertainty, the basis for any
independence claim, explicit nonclaims, and the consequence of being wrong.

These fields cannot be averaged into one number. Increasing confidence means
reducing or bounding relevant failure paths for a named claim. Agreement
between checks that share the same blind spot does not reduce the risk
contributed by that shared blind spot. A proved property can coexist with
uncertain performance, incomplete workload coverage, and an untested security
claim.

### Connecting Requirements to Checks

Passing every check that ran does not establish requirement satisfaction.
For each declared material requirement or hard constraint, the project must
name the artifact and conditions, acceptance criterion, check path suited to
the property, empirical uncertainty or formal status, shared assumptions, and
uncovered remainder. A missing or unqualified mapping leaves that requirement
unresolved even when every other performed check passes. Passing all mapped
checks still does not establish that the requirement set is complete.

A confidence interval can support a statistical performance or reliability
requirement when the target population, sampling assumptions, risk criterion,
and decision margin are declared. Some yield and manufacturing requirements are
also statistical and must retain their population and variation model. A hard
timing, power, or design-rule acceptance limit instead requires the project's
designated signoff method to resolve the acceptance rule under named modes,
corners, modeled variation, and uncertainty. A favorable point estimate is not
a hard-limit pass. If the designated analysis cannot establish the acceptable
side of the limit under those conditions, the requirement remains unresolved.

The unexecuted Lighthouse cache study makes the mappings concrete without
inventing a candidate result.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse requirements remain unresolved for different reasons"}
**Context.** The prospective study names request and interface legality, SRAM
area and access time, 99th-percentile frame time, a 3\ W subsystem power target,
and functional, protocol, security, reliability, and system-level XR behavior.

**Required checks.** Request legality, SRAM limits, frame time, and power need
versioned request and artifact checks, complete SRAM results with model and
process, voltage, and temperature conditions, matched frame-time measurements
with uncertainty, and a qualified subsystem power result. The remaining
properties need simulation or named formal checks that observe each declared
requirement.

**Status.** The prospective study has no translated inputs, retained SRAM or
power artifacts, matched frame records, parser evidence, or uncertainty. Those
four mappings are unqualified, neither passes nor failures. Functional,
protocol, security, reliability, and system-level XR requirements have no check
path and remain uncovered. All candidate choices remain open.

**Takeaway.** An unqualified result lacks the record needed to interpret its
check. An uncovered requirement lacks a suitable check. Human review can expose
either gap, but it cannot supply a missing measurement or proof.
:::

### What Different Checks Establish

A valid measurement may still address the wrong property. Syntax checks,
functional simulation, model checking, performance simulation, synthesis,
timing analysis, power analysis, and post-silicon characterization answer
different questions. Their strength is not a single ordering from weak to
strong. A parser can conclusively reject an illegal request while an expensive
timing run says nothing about functional correctness. Representative check
boundaries make that mismatch explicit without implying a universal ordering
(@tbl-check-scope).

| **Check class** | **What it can support within stated conditions** | **What it does not establish by itself** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Syntax and interface** | Legal encoding, type, schema, instruction set architecture (ISA), application binary interface (ABI), or protocol form. | Functional behavior, performance, physical feasibility, or system intent. |
| **Functional simulation and testing** | Behavior for exercised stimuli and observed properties. | Unexercised behaviors, physical timing, power, or unspecified security properties. |
| **Formal property and equivalence checks** | A stated property over a modeled transition system, or a stated relation between two artifacts. | Whether the property captures intent, whether assumptions match deployment, or unrelated properties. |
| **Architecture performance and power models** | Quantities represented by the model for the declared workload and configuration. | Effects the abstraction omits or behavior outside its validated region. |
| **Implementation and physical analysis** | Timing, area, power, integrity, or rule results for the modeled design, constraints, modes, and corners. | Missing constraints, unmodeled conditions, functional intent, or manufactured variation outside the analysis. |
| **Post-silicon and operational measurement** | Behavior of sampled parts and systems under measured conditions. | Every manufactured part, workload, environment, lifetime condition, or unmeasured property. |

: **A check is decisive only for the property it observes.** More cost or later
placement in a flow does not widen that property.
{#tbl-check-scope tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

The checks are complementary rather than a hierarchy from weak to strong. A later
or more expensive check can settle one implementation property while leaving
functional intent, security, or an earlier interface obligation untouched.
Architecture claims therefore need coverage across the material properties,
not merely progress to the most expensive available tool stage.

The property a check observes is only half of the measurement plan. The
intended use of its result also matters. A mistaken local ranking can waste
evaluation budget and change which candidates the search examines. A mistaken
result used to revise a shared artifact or interface can propagate across
hardware, software, verification, and integration work. The feedback plan
should therefore grow with the cost of being wrong and the difficulty of
reversing the result's technical consequences
(@tbl-feedback-by-consequence).

| **Intended use of the result** | **Consequence if the result is wrong** | **Feedback plan should include** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Choose the next local evaluation** | A candidate is explored unnecessarily, a promising one is deferred, or scarce tool time is spent on the wrong question. | Candidate identity, a matched comparator, known proxy limits, and enough precision to choose the next check. |
| **Revise a shared implementation or interface** | Hardware, software, verification, or integration work may inherit the error. | Relevant regression and compatibility checks, explicit shared assumptions, and a different check path for critical properties where practical. |
| **Support a high-consequence technical conclusion** | The error may survive into later work where it is expensive to find or reverse. | Checks covering each material claim, uncertainty relative to the decision margin, a sufficiently different path where shared failure matters, and explicit unmeasured properties. |

: **The feedback plan follows consequence and reversibility.** More costly
checks are not automatically more informative. The plan must cover the claims
and failure modes that matter for the result's intended use.
{#tbl-feedback-by-consequence tbl-colwidths="[27,32,41]"}

Once a result can propagate into shared artifacts or expensive work, a wrong
interpretation becomes harder to reverse. A wrong local choice may waste tool
time. A wrong shared-interface revision can spread through hardware, software,
verification, and integration, while a wrong high-consequence conclusion can
survive into expensive work. The feedback plan must grow with that exposure,
but technical support still does not authorize the resulting action.

### Describing the Check and Its Limits

Some architecture results depend on confidential workloads, design data, or
tool flows. They can support an internal conclusion when an authorized reviewer
can inspect the complete record and challenge its method, scope, uncertainty,
and limits. A public claim must remain within what public material or an audit
by a reviewer with access to the protected record can establish.
Confidentiality does not turn a production report into an independently
replayable comparison.

Three questions that many tool reports omit make a check reviewable.

**Coverage.** Which failures can the check observe, and which relevant failures
leave no signal?

**Possible error direction.** Under the declared model and conditions, is the
result known to be conservative, optimistic, or neither? This must be
established for the particular flow. A pre-route estimate is not always
optimistic, and a deterministic computation is not automatically a safe
bound.

Static timing analysis illustrates why the error direction is conditional.
Cadence documents concurrent multi-mode, multi-corner analysis and statistical
on-chip variation analysis in Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus]. The architecture
lesson is broader than those product capabilities. A result may be deliberately
pessimistic, but that claim applies only to the declared timing mode, process,
voltage, and temperature corner, derates, constraints, and modeled effects. A
pass or failure is meaningful within those conditions, not as a universal
bound. Sampled simulation has a different shape. A failing trace rejects the
exercised behavior, but a passing sample says nothing about unexercised stimuli
or properties absent from the testbench.

**Shared assumptions.** Which specifications, models, data, workloads,
constraints, code, and tool paths are shared with the producer or with another
check? A different program name or model instance does not create
independence.

Agreement adds information only when the second path changes the relevant
failure source (@fig-independent-checks). The alternative need not claim
perfect independence. It must observe the disputed property through a
sufficiently different path to reduce a known shared failure.

![**A second check adds information only when it changes the relevant failure
path.** A critic using the same assumptions can repeat the producer's omission.
A claim-specific check based on a sufficiently different model or measurement
path can reduce that correlation, but its remaining shared inputs and blind
spots must still be recorded.](images/ch7_independent_checks){#fig-independent-checks
width="92%" fig-alt="Two-column diagram. A producer and
critic sharing the same assumptions lead to correlated agreement. A producer
and a claim-specific check with a different measurement path lead to a
bounded challenge, with remaining shared assumptions explicitly retained."}

In the left path, the candidate producer and critic use the same specification
and model, so agreement remains correlated. In the right path, a claim-specific
check observes the disputed property differently and produces a bounded
challenge. The note beneath both
paths sets the limit. Some assumptions and inputs may remain shared, so a
different path can reduce correlation without proving independence.

Two uses of a second path should not be conflated. Independent qualification
of the same record challenges extraction, arithmetic, or bookkeeping. A
separate parser can recover a value from the raw report, and an independent
calculation can check its aggregation. Both may still inherit the original
tool's model, workload, and constraints. They strengthen confidence in what
that tool returned without testing whether the tool observed the right
physical property.

A materially different observation path challenges more of the claim. Another
simulator with different models, an RTL property check, a physical-design
measurement, or a direct hardware observation may expose an error that record
requalification cannot. It also has shared assumptions that must be named.
The useful question is not whether the second path deserves the label
*independent*. It is which failure source changes and which one remains shared.

Separate teams can fail together on the same hard inputs. Knight and Leveson
found correlated failures among independently developed program versions,
showing that separate implementation does not guarantee independent error
[@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. The same warning applies to a generator and
critic that share a foundation model, training data, objective, or
specification. Agreement can be useful corroboration without being an
independent check.

LLM evaluation supplies a narrower warning. Experiments have found that an LLM
evaluator can favor its own text generations over alternatives that human
raters judge to be equally good [@PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference]. That
result concerns evaluation of generated text. It does not establish a universal
same-family bias when a model critiques RTL, simulator traces, timing reports,
or physical-design results. Knight and Leveson's broader lesson still governs
the architecture claim. A separate implementation or critic name is not enough;
the check must change the failure path relevant to the property.

The missing-property case is different. Spectre and Meltdown exploited
microarchitectural side effects that ordinary functional correctness does not
constrain [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. More functional
tests of ordinary program outputs would not settle confidentiality. Tests
designed around leakage can bear on the security claim, while an ordinary
performance suite cannot.

Checks also need checks. Mutation testing injects faults and reports which ones
a suite detects [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints]. A mutation score says
something only about the injected fault model, and equivalent or unobservable
mutants need careful handling. For model-generated assertions and testbenches, the
useful fault set should resemble errors the generator actually makes rather
than only traditional hand-written mistakes.

A check can be valid for the property it observes and still be only a proxy
for the architecture objective. Functional simulation may establish agreement
for tested inputs without settling performance, while a cycle estimate may
rank candidates without establishing timing closure. The remaining question
is how far the cheaper observation can carry the stronger claim.

A reviewer can support a technical conclusion only after the project maps the
identified material requirements, qualifies the supporting artifacts and
results, resolves uncertainty relative to the acceptance margins, and uses a
sufficiently different failure path where the consequence warrants it. The
requirement set may still be incomplete, so residual unknowns and explicit
nonclaims remain part of the conclusion. This technical support does not
authorize architecture commitment. It establishes which next technical action
the feedback can justify.

## Routing the Next Technical Action

Once a qualified result supports, contradicts, or leaves a named claim
unresolved, feedback points to the object that needs attention and the next
eligible technical action. The signal does not prescribe its own update, and
the technical action does not by itself authorize an architecture commitment.

An incomplete or invalid execution record routes directly to the environment
before verification or feedback. The remaining cross-cutting statuses direct
attention to the object implicated by the qualified or verified result
(@tbl-feedback-destinations). Formal statuses use the more specific actions in
@tbl-formal-result-status.

| **Established status** | **Object needing attention** | **Resulting move** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Invalid execution** | Tool-connected environment | Repair extraction, state, lineage, or invocation before interpreting the candidate. |
| **Wrong represented state** | Design representation | Correct the represented problem and invalidate results that used the wrong state. |
| **Qualified architecture effect** | Project record; design owner if revision is supported | Record the bounded result and revise the design only when it supports that move. |
| **Proxy outside support** | Approach choice or qualification study | Recalibrate, narrow, replace, or stop using the proxy. Do not create training labels automatically. |
| **Missing constraint or assumption** | Study formulation or representation | Record the rationale and repair the object that omitted the requirement. |
| **Resolved outcome, unresolved mechanism** | Study formulation | Preserve the result and add a distinguishing contrast before using the explanation to guide another change. |
| **Unresolved comparison** | Measurement plan or study formulation | Improve the contrast, precision target, observation budget, or stopping rule. |
| **Difference below the decision margin** | Project record | Preserve the result without forcing a design or model update. |
| **Accepted bounded exception** | Project record and responsible owner | Preserve the failed status, scope, rationale, compensating control, residual risk, expiration, and reopening condition. |

: **Established status determines the next technical move.** Execution failure
routes directly to the environment before verification or feedback. Qualified
or verified results then direct repair, recording, revision, requalification,
or no change at the relevant object.
{#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[32,25,43]"}

Qualification can point to the object that needs repair or can use the result,
while unsupported inferences remain open.
That direction need not produce a design change. A difference below the
declared margin updates the project record, a proof discharges only its stated
property, and a waiver preserves a failure as a scoped exception. No route turns
a tool failure or unresolved comparison into a training label automatically.

::: {.callout-field-note title="An illustrative timing return produces a bounded action"}
**The expectation.** A qualified timing return should support a bounded claim
and eligible repair, not a conclusion about the whole pipeline.

**In practice.** This example is illustrative, not empirical project evidence.
For mapped netlist `CPU-NL-17`, constraint set `CPU-SDC-17`, and corner
`SS_0P72V_125C`, the return for path `EX-MEM-P17` reports
$-0.04\,\mathrm{ns}$ setup slack from `U_EX/alu_sum_reg[17]/Q` to
`U_MEM/addr_reg[17]/D`. Complete tool status,
constrained endpoints, clock model, derates, and report lineage qualify the
value for that named setup check. The bounded claim is that this path violates
its zero-slack setup requirement under the declared conditions. It says nothing
about hold timing, function, power, another corner, or global feasibility. That
claim makes moving a pipeline boundary or reducing logic depth eligible,
followed by logical equivalence, functional regression, and setup-and-hold
reruns for every affected mode and corner.

**The lesson.** Retain the failing path and conditions with the repair
rationale. Reopen the result whenever the netlist, constraint set, clock model,
derates, or affected path endpoints change.
:::

A qualified status makes a technical action eligible; it does not schedule the
next attempt. An invalid execution permits environment repair, a qualified
hard-constraint violation permits candidate rejection or revision, and an
unresolved comparison permits a better measurement or contrast. A retry is
eligible only when a linked attempt could resolve the pending decision within
the remaining budget. @sec-running-the-loop owns how eligible actions are
scheduled, repeated, budgeted, and stopped. This chapter establishes what the
signal can justify. Defects that block validity or required correctness still
take precedence over optional performance refinement.

When two feedback sources appear to conflict, first align the candidate,
property, conditions, versions, and aggregation. The signals may concern
different scopes rather than contradict one claim. If they still conflict,
inspect shared assumptions and known error directions, then choose a
distinguishing check targeted at the disputed property. When neither result
can be shown to supersede the other, preserve both as unresolved. Do not
average incompatible signals or select a source by prestige.

A reviewer's observation is feedback. Approval is a separate, authorized
project action. Neither makes an unsupported result valid. Approval may accept
bounded residual risk, but it cannot supply a missing measurement or check.
Final architecture commitment remains separate and belongs to
@sec-what-architect-owns.

Some failed checks can remain open under a bounded waiver accepted by an
authorized owner. The waiver does not turn the failed result into a pass. It
retains the failed check, rationale, exact scope, responsible owner,
compensating check or control, residual risk, expiration or review condition,
and reopening trigger. Waiver support in a physical-verification flow can
preserve waived design-rule violations and their associated text. Siemens
documents this behavior for Calibre Auto-Waivers, which applies the records
across later design rule checking (DRC) runs
[@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers]. The technical record belongs here. Authority to
accept the residual risk belongs to
@sec-what-architect-owns.

Routing ends with an eligible action. A qualified result becomes learning only
when the current run or project changes, or when later work retains a lesson,
because of that result.

## How Returned Signals Change the Work

One feedback path stays within the current run. A qualified SRAM
access-time violation can make the predeclared no-dispatch action eligible for
that cache candidate. An architect or method may then evaluate a smaller cache,
revise the memory organization, or end that branch through the run controls in
@sec-running-the-loop.

Some results outlive the run and change project state. An interface
counterexample that has been reviewed and shown realizable under the intended
conditions can add a retained protocol constraint and regression test, correct
the represented state, withdraw qualification from an affected component, and
record which interface change would reopen earlier results.

A result may also remain useful after the current project ends. The qualified
range, held-out checks, and failed cases for a cache proxy can be preserved as
scoped artifacts and lessons. Another project may reuse them, but it must
re-establish the conclusions under the transfer conditions described in
@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack.

Learning here means one of these justified changes to what the work does or
retains, not an automatic model update.

Project learning and model learning are different. A design constraint,
contradicted comparison, supported intermediate effect, or supported mechanism
can update project state without becoming training data. A model update needs a
named target, usable labels, scope, and acceptance test. Tool failures,
unmatched results, and unresolved comparisons should not become simple pass or
fail labels.

Architects already maintain verification plans, requirements traceability,
regression and coverage databases, signoff reports, waiver records, and
change-impact tracking. The cumulative study record indexes those mechanisms
and links them to the claims and decisions they support. It does not replace
them with a parallel workflow or another bureaucracy.

### Updating a Learned Component

An updated model or proxy is a new component version within the design system
[@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. In architecture work, that version change can
invalidate candidate rankings, proxy scope, and cached search decisions that
depended on the previous component. Architecture search also chooses which
candidates receive expensive labels, so the labeled outcomes are
policy-selected and the missing outcomes are not random. Active learning studies
how a method chooses which example to label next [@Settles2009ActiveLearning];
@sec-data-representations-world-models introduced the corresponding
selective-acquisition problem for architecture data. Learning only from returned
labels can reinforce the regions the current search already favors and preserve
its blind spots.

Before the component reenters the design process, the project records the
update data, acquisition policy, and retained selection decisions, including
candidates that did not receive labels. The project then tests failure-relevant
cases and previously qualified cases or strata that were not used for the
update, repeats the decision-relevant error, ranking, or proxy-qualification
checks, and looks for regressions. Randomized or stratified audit evaluations
should probe cases outside the policy's choices where practical.

When acceptance results steer subsequent updates, repeated use turns those
cases into development data, just as adaptive reuse can overfit a holdout set
[@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. The project must therefore keep acceptance cases
untouched or refresh them. The updated component should remain outside the
active process until it passes a shadow evaluation that does not steer candidate
selection, or a sufficiently independent acceptance path. It then reenters with
revised qualification scope and reopening conditions rather than inheriting the
previous version's scope. Passing these checks qualifies the new component
version for its declared use. It does not inherit the architecture conclusions
supported by the old version.

### Reopening and Requalifying

A project reopens an old interpretation when changed conditions require
requalification. A changed workload, software image, model, tool, operating
condition, candidate revision, artifact, interface, requirement, proxy
calibration result, or contrary observation can reopen dependent claims without
predetermining the next revision. The project identifies which binding or
relationship may no longer hold. It does not silently invalidate unrelated
results.

Distribution shift occurs when the data-generating conditions encountered in
use differ from those represented during development or qualification
[@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. In architecture work, the change can be
a new workload mix, movement into a different candidate region, or a new
distribution of process, voltage, and temperature conditions. A *drift signal*
is an observed change over time in those conditions or in the proxy's residuals,
interval coverage, or ranking stability. Such a signal does not identify its
cause, and it does not by itself authorize retraining.

Many changes remain within the same project and current target decision. A
tightened timing constraint may reopen only the requirement comparison and
margin that used the old limit; a qualified timing measurement can remain intact
when its artifact and conditions have not changed. A revised reset or interface
version may reopen the functional, formal, and integration checks that consumed
it while leaving unrelated measurements intact. The project traces each claim
and check to the workload, tool or model, artifact, condition, interface, and
requirement it depends on. It reruns the minimum adequate affected checks and
keeps an unaffected claim only with a recorded rationale.

A candidate, configuration, tool, or operating-condition mismatch can make an
affected execution record stale and require lineage repair or a rerun of the
same check. Changed workload populations, phase coverage, or movement among
candidate cases can require new sampling and repeated qualification.
Deteriorating proxy-reference residuals, interval coverage, or ranking stability
can require narrowing,
recalibrating, replacing, or stopping the proxy. Relearning is one possible
response only when the proxy is a learned component and an independent
acceptance test exists.

The project faces a new target decision when the objective's meaning, legal
action space, artifact boundary, or acceptance semantics change enough to alter
the decision itself. Determining what prior results carry into that target is a
transfer problem rather than selective requalification within the current
decision (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). Until that boundary is crossed, the
project preserves each old result and its scope, names the affected dependencies
and minimum adequate checks, and lets the new evidence determine the update.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Execution failure is not candidate failure.** A setup, license, invocation,
  or parse failure says that the measurement path failed; rejecting the
  candidate or using that return as a training label creates a false negative.

- **A proxy is valid only within its qualified range.** Improving an IPC,
  energy, wirelength, or congestion estimate can still degrade post-route
  power, performance, and area (PPA), correctness, or the real-workload
  objective unless later checks preserve the result.

- **Adaptation feedback is not fresh acceptance evidence.** Selecting labels
  for adaptation or repeatedly reusing a holdout can make a model appear to
  improve while preserving the blind spots and invalidation conditions that
  the reused evidence can no longer test.

## Open Questions

Qualified feedback still leaves open how an architecture study should judge
imperfect checks, detect shared blind spots, and retain useful learning without
extending a result beyond its support.

**Qualifying proxies and checks.** A fast or apparently independent check is
useful only when its scope, blind spots, and dependence on other checks are
understood.

- **How can an architecture study determine when a proxy is accurate enough to
  guide a design decision?** A proxy can have low average error while
  misranking candidates or hiding a constraint violation near the decision
  boundary. The unresolved difficulty is determining where its error changes
  the architecture decision and where a stronger check is worth its cost.

- **How can correlated failure be measured across apparently independent
  checks in an AI-assisted architecture study?** Different tools, models,
  and reviewers can still inherit the same specification error, workload blind
  spot, library, or training source. Agreement provides little protection when
  the supposedly independent paths share the cause of failure. Research must
  identify dependence that matters to the architecture claim and determine
  when a genuinely different observation path is needed.

- **How can model-generated tests and properties be checked for semantic omissions
  or insufficient strength?** Generated verification collateral may be
  syntactically valid and nonvacuous while omitting required protocol, timing,
  reset, security, or progress behavior. The hard problem is deciding whether
  a test or property is strong enough for the architecture claim rather than
  merely capable of producing a pass.

**Learning and requalifying feedback.** Qualified results can still be biased
by which candidates were checked and can become stale when project conditions
change.

- **How can an AI-assisted architecture system update a learned component
  reliably when its own search policy determines which outcomes become
  labels?** The system observes
  outcomes only for candidates its own search policy chooses to evaluate, so
  later updates can reinforce the regions it already favors and miss unexplored
  failures. Some independent sampling may reveal that bias, but the unresolved
  question is how much feedback can be trusted when stronger checks are delayed
  or expensive.

- **How can an AI-assisted architecture system select the minimum adequate
  checks to rerun after a within-study change?** A small design change can
  invalidate several claims, yet the dependencies between artifacts,
  measurements, and checks are rarely complete. Repeating every check wastes
  scarce simulator and implementation time, while incomplete impact analysis
  can leave stale support in place. The research problem is to find the smallest
  set of renewed checks that reestablishes support for the affected claims.

## Conclusion {#sec-trust-boundary-conclusion}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Let only qualified results drive the next architecture action"}
A raw return becomes usable only after the project establishes what ran, which
candidate and property it concerns, the design, workload, and tool conditions,
and the comparison or formal claim it supports. Use only that qualified result
to select a repair, design revision, additional check, or retained project
lesson, and preserve its limits and reopening conditions. Retraining is one
possible response, not the definition of learning.
:::

An architect can turn a returned signal into a bounded architecture result only
after establishing execution and artifact validity, qualifying the relevant
measurement or formal status, and matching the check to the claim. That status
controls the eligible technical action. Learning retains the result, its
reason, its limits, and the condition that would reopen it.

Qualification determines which actions are eligible. A multi-step study
must still decide when to schedule and stop them without losing state,
cost, lineage, or rationale. @sec-running-the-loop
explains how to orchestrate those
decisions.
